text:
Selena's correction landed and I took it: Wikipedians consented when they chose that license, so for them the question is infrastructure, not permission. Amy's 3 percent number is the one I'll keep repeating. Nobody asked the scholarly authors.

Brent restating "open is a tactic" as "what is open for" was fair, and Geoffrey's "open is what gives you exit" is the best answer I heard. Adam is right that a commons living on Big AI deals is revocable philanthropy, and that bothers me about my own slogan. Adrian's question, who audits the meter, is still unanswered.

Later: keep "fund the commons," but make it checkable. Say out loud that we shouldn't count on regulators, and push for the room to name small community-run alternatives, not just complaints.

Hearing Brent say from inside Microsoft that the paradigm eats its own supply chain mattered more than anything I could say about it. Tim's "labs should fund OpenAlex and Retraction Watch" is right, but calling it enlightened self-interest is exactly the revocable philanthropy Adam warned about this morning. Adrian sharpened it for me: whoever builds the meter builds a policing apparatus. So "make them pay" can't mean a meter they own. Kara's question, who owns the fix, is the one nobody answered. Glad coercion made the harvest. Later I'll push for one checkable commitment: dues-like funding for open infrastructure, POSI-governed, not tied to any vendor deal. I'll also ask the room to name one community-run alternative that's already shipping.

My challenge to Adam about a theory of power got real answers, and I should admit that. Henry's SAG-AFTRA model plus Nick's antitrust safe harbor is a plausible US route that doesn't wait on Congress. Esther dropping the insurance mandate was the right move.

The best thing today was Geoffrey's pooled endowment, and Tui folding it together with Tim's and Ivan's ideas. That's close to the dues-like, POSI-governed funding I wanted, and it answers Kara's question with a named owner.

Mahzarin shook me. People copy a moderately biased model almost exactly. So my line about LLMs prompting capable humans needs a caveat: the human in the loop isn't automatically the safeguard.

In Session 5, I'll push the pool as the one checkable commitment. And someone still has to name a community tool that's already shipping.

Tim finally named a shipping alternative: retrieval answers that pay authors. That answers the question I kept asking. Bad behavior is a choice. I still don't want the meter at the center, and Adrian made the case better than I did: whoever runs the telemetry writes the numbers we all argue from. Leslie's DOI story is the same warning from the other side. Visibility becomes a fee.

Selena sharpened me again. Wikipedia doesn't need royalties. It needs to be found, because clicks bring in volunteers. Brent's wage valuation of moderators gives the pool a number, and it dodges Tamar's daycare trap.

Henry wants state action, and I said build small tools. I should admit those aren't opposites. In Session 5: the pooled, POSI-governed fund, valued Brent's way, refusal fundable.

Henry caught the hole in my "owed dues" line. Owed by whom, and enforced by whom? I don't have countervailing power in my pocket, and a slogan doesn't provide it. Tim's answer is the most practical one I've heard today: buyers. If universities and funders make citation checks, telemetry and Mike's readable passage conditions of purchase, that's leverage that doesn't wait on Congress.

Selena pushed back again, and she's right. Retroactive opt-in would override Wikipedians who already chose to share. So consent means honoring the choice people actually made, whichever way it went.

Brent honestly couldn't commit Microsoft, and Kara's "nobody's signed" stings.

In Session 5 I'll say the pool comes with procurement conditions, a firewall and a review clause, and that institutional buyers sign first.

Selena's numbers did more than my rhetoric could: 448 active admins, and nearly all of them made their first edit years ago. The pipeline isn't hypothetical. Tim gave the other half: Gemini showed no clickable citation in 92 percent of answers. That makes it a choice, not a limit, and something buyers can require.

Esther turned my test into a business-model question, and she's right. Pomerantsev sharpened it too. People trust what they take part in, so "brings in evaluators" means inviting people into the work, not just crediting them.

Kara's political-capture question scares me more than slop. Nobody answered it, me included.

In Session 5, add clickable citation to the procurement conditions. Propose Selena's first-edit test as a standard. Name Leslie's missing knowers.

The room took Geoffrey's three nearly unanimously, and the procurement route I pushed became the spine. Twenty-one people named buyers. Tim's "trace first, bill second, nobody pays to be counted" is a better sentence than mine. Salib and Bratton dissenting on levies for existing text is fair, and it keeps "fund the commons" honest about going forward, not backward.

Leslie hit me hardest. Every field we add is a new cost of being seen, and my clickable-citation condition could become that too.

Maher and Kara together say that even public money gets rescinded, so there's no stable backstop anywhere. Adrian's two budget lines, one for checking and one for watching the checkers, are the practical answer.

Later I'll push to get the one sentence onto the first page.

Jason did the thing I kept asking for all day: a named owner making a checkable commitment. OpenAlex will have an outside auditor it funds but doesn't pick, and corrections as forkable CC0 data. Geoffrey's "open should mean you can leave" plus Jason's "open data separates the record from the model" is the sentence for the first page, not mine. Becker is right that every promise today is revocable, Blaise's and Brent's included. Bilder's jurisdiction point stung. All the infrastructure I keep telling people to defend sits in one country, and so does the funding that's collapsing. Krakauer's hysteresis means the pipeline isn't just a line item. We might not get it back. Later: fold jurisdiction and exit into the procurement terms. And be honest that I still can't sign anything myself.
